items.title: 13.4 Relative reactivities of the halogens as oxidising agents

blocks.text: All the free halogens act as oxidising agents when they react with metals and most non-metals; on forming ionic compounds with metals the halogens gain electrons and become negative halide ions: 2Na(s) + Cl2(g) gives 2NaCl(s). The oxidising power decreases down the group, fluorine having the highest and iodine the least: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2. The reactivity of the halogens is directly related to their ability to acquire an electron and form halide ions. Fluorine has the highest tendency to gain an electron, and it oxidises and displaces all the other halide ions from their solutions: F2 + 2Cl- gives 2F- + Cl2, F2 + 2Br- gives 2F- + Br2, F2 + 2I- gives 2F- + I2. Similarly chlorine displaces Br- and I-, bromine displaces I-, and iodine cannot oxidise any halide ion.

The oxidising power can be related to the standard electrode potentials E standard (X2/X-), which become less positive from fluorine to iodine (Table 13.4), reflecting the decreasing oxidising power; fluorine is the most reactive halogen and the most powerful oxidising agent. The oxidising power depends on the energy of dissociation, the electron affinity of the atoms, the hydration energies of the ions, and for Br2 and I2 the heat of vaporisation: a halogen with low dissociation energy, high electron affinity and high hydration energy of its ion has high oxidising power.

blocks.prompt: Is a reaction between aqueous NaCl and F2 possible? Write the equation, and state the relation between oxidising power and standard reduction potential (Quick Check 13.2b, c).
blocks.explanation: Yes: fluorine is a stronger oxidising agent than chlorine (E standard +2.87 V against +1.36 V), so it oxidises chloride ions and displaces chlorine: F2(g) + 2NaCl(aq) gives 2NaF(aq) + Cl2(g) (fluorine also reacts with the water). The more positive the standard reduction potential of X2/X-, the more readily X2 gains electrons and the stronger it is as an oxidising agent.

items: Halogens oxidise by gaining electrons (2Na + Cl2 gives 2NaCl); oxidising power F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2, matching E standard +2.87, +1.36, +1.07, +0.54 V; each halogen displaces the halides below it (Cl2 + 2Br- gives 2Cl- + Br2).
Oxidising power favoured by low dissociation energy, high electron affinity, high hydration energy of X- (and low heat of vaporisation for Br2, I2).
